title: Any idea how to properly backtest an AI trading bot?
author: orid7
selftext:
My trading bots so far are plain rules, so backtesting them is easy. Now I want an LLM making the calls, and I can't see how to test it honestly.

The model has read the news from the period I would test on, so it already knows how 2024 ended. The same prompt gives different answers on different runs. And two years of daily calls is not cheap to replay.

The only honest option I can see is running it live on paper for months and waiting.

If you run an LLM in your trading loop, how did you get confidence it works?

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
Your 2024 concern puts a limit on what historical returns can establish: restricting the news you supply doesn't remove knowledge already in the model. Hiding dates and tickers could probe that problem, but wouldn't prove it's gone.

Before paying for two years of daily calls, I'd repeat a small, deliberately varied set of decision snapshots and measure how often the action and position size change. Include identical snapshots in fresh sessions so conversation history doesn't confound the comparison. That can tell you whether one expensive replay would even be representative. Then use historical runs to catch implementation failures, and prospective paper decisions to assess performance on unseen events. Specify upfront whether deployment uses one answer or aggregates several; test that exact procedure.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
you've named the real problem, the model has already read the ending. two partial fixes and neither is clean. one is to shrink the model down to a component that can't cheat: don't ask it to make the call, ask it to turn a headline into a structured label (direction, magnitude, confidence) and backtest the labels with a plain rule on top. leakage is still there but it's bounded to the labeling, and you can measure it by feeding the same headlines with tickers and dates scrubbed and seeing whether the labels shift. the other is to accept the only clean sample starts today, and run it forward on paper with the prompt frozen and every call logged with the exact context it saw, because the second you edit the prompt you've started a new experiment.

on the nondeterminism, run each day three times at temperature zero and treat disagreement as no trade. smaller sample, but the calls left are the ones the model actually believes.

I built Quantradin after hitting this same wall. it's a backtester and paper desk with honest fills that an agent or Claude can drive over MCP, so the forward test logs itself, and there's no charge for it.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
*The knowledge-cutoff leakage is the real killer, and it's subtler than "the model knows how 2024 ended" — even if you tell it "pretend it's June 2024," a model trained on data through 2025 has absorbed correlations from knowing the outcome, which can bias its reasoning in ways you can't fully prompt away. The only clean fix is using a model whose training cutoff predates your test window entirely, or — more practically — never letting the model see raw dates/context that could leak future knowledge, and instead feeding it strictly point-in-time retrieved data (only the news/prices that existed as of that simulated day) rather than trusting it to "forget" what it already knows.*

*For the non-determinism problem: run each decision point N times (5-10) at the same point-in-time context and look at the distribution of calls, not a single run — if the model flips between buy/hold/sell on identical inputs, that's itself the finding (the strategy isn't stable enough to trust), and averaging or majority-voting across samples gives you a more honest backtest than a single noisy run pretending to be deterministic.*

*On cost: you don't need daily calls for two years if the actual decision-relevant events are sparser than that — batch your point-in-time context construction once, then only call the LLM on days where something changed materially (new filing, news event, technical trigger), which cuts both cost and the surface area for cutoff leakage since you're not replaying past dates where nothing happened. That point-in-time data assembly — guaranteeing the model only ever sees what was knowable at that exact moment — is exactly the discipline EventTrader's event-driven pipeline enforces, since lookahead bias from data that "arrives" before its actual timestamp is the single most common way backtests lie.* [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)

comments.author: CODE_HEIST
comments.body: historical replay can test implementation, but it can’t fully remove pretraining leakage. i’d freeze the prompt and decision rule, run identical snapshots several times to measure action and sizing variance, then start a prospective Paper test with the exact context and every abstention logged. comparing that against a simple deterministic baseline should reveal whether the LLM is adding stable information or just extra variability.
